_note: Case counts: the number taught in each language's standard grammar. Experts disagree for some (Hungarian 17 to 27, or none if the endings are counted as postpositions); languages with very large disagreements (Tsez, Archi, Basque, Lezgian) left out. Owner approved the list 2026-11-06. Audio built by build_cases.py.
title: Ranking Languages by How Many Grammar Cases They Have
subtitle: THE ENDINGS THAT SHOW WHO DOES WHAT TO WHOM
outro: Which language's cases drive you crazy?

items.name: Hungarian
items.lit: house → in the house → out of the house → into the house
cards: 18 cases. Endings do the job of English words like in, on, from and to.
One word, many endings: háznál 'at the house', házhoz 'towards the house', házon 'on the house'.

items.name: Finnish
items.lit: Finland → Finland's → (I speak) Finnish → in Finland → from Finland
cards: 15 cases, and a noun can take every one of them in the singular and the plural.
There is even a case for 'without': rahatta means 'without money'.

items.name: Estonian
items.lit: year → in the year → from the year → (two) years
cards: 14 cases. Estonian is a close relative of Finnish.
Many cases are just an ending added to the word: aastal 'in the year', aastast 'from the year'.

items.name: Tamil
items.lit: house → in the house → to the house
cards: 8 cases. Tamil grammarians already listed them about 2,000 years ago.
Tamil is one of the oldest languages still spoken today, in India, Sri Lanka and Singapore.

items.name: Polish
items.lit: house → of the house → to the house → with the house → in the house
cards: 7 cases, and every noun changes its ending for them.
Even names change: Marta becomes Marty, Marcie, Martę or Martą.

items.name: Lithuanian
items.lit: house → of the house → to the house → the house (object) → in the house
cards: 7 cases. Many of its endings are close to those of ancient Sanskrit.
It is often called the most old-fashioned Indo-European language still spoken.

items.name: Russian
items.lit: house → to the house → (about) the house
cards: 6 cases, with different endings for masculine, feminine and neuter words.
Numbers change the case too: один дом (one house), два дома (two houses), пять домов (five houses).

items.name: Turkish
cards: 6 cases, made by sticking endings onto the word.
You just heard two of them: Ankara'ya gittim 'I went to Ankara', then Ankara'da 'in Ankara'.

items.name: German
cards: 4 cases, shown mostly by the word for 'the'.
Der Mann (the man) can become den Mann, dem Mann or des Mannes.

items.name: Arabic
items.lit: a book, in its three cases

items.name: English
cards: 0 cases for nouns: 'the house' stays 'the house' whatever it does in the sentence.
Old English had 4 cases. Today only pronouns keep them: I, me, my.
